intro: Here's a Dockerfile for a Python application.
notes: Use a slim base, install dependencies via requirements.txt (or pip install -e . for an editable package), and prefer COPY over ADD. Multi-stage builds shrink the final image.

languages.bash:
FROM python:3.12-slim

# Set the working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies first (caches the layer when requirements.txt changes)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy the application code
COPY . .

# Non-root user (security)
RUN useradd --create-home appuser
USER appuser

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 8000

# Run the app
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

# Build:   docker build -t myapp .
# Run:     docker run -p 8000:8000 myapp

intro: Here's a docker-compose.yml for a web app with a database.
notes: Compose orchestrates multi-container apps. Services get their own network; the app reaches the db at the service name (db:5432). Volumes persist data across restarts.

languages.bash:
version: '3.9'

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
      POSTGRES_DB: myapp
    volumes:
      - db_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ['CMD-SHELL', 'pg_isready -U app']
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - '8000:8000'
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://app:secret@db:5432/myapp
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    volumes:
      - .:/app          # live-reload during development

volumes:
  db_data:

# Up:      docker compose up
# Build:   docker compose up --build
# Logs:    docker compose logs -f web

intro: Here's a GitHub Actions workflow that runs tests on push.
notes: Workflows live in .github/workflows/*.yml. on: triggers (push, pull_request); jobs run in parallel by default — use needs: to chain them. setup-python caches dependencies for you.

languages.bash:
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'
          cache: 'pip'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: |
          pip install -r requirements-dev.txt

      - name: Run tests
        run: pytest

      - name: Lint
        run: ruff check .

  deploy:
    needs: test            # only after tests pass
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Deploy
        run: ./deploy.sh
        env:
          API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }}

intro: Here's a .gitignore for a Python project.
notes: Ignore generated files, caches, virtualenvs, and secrets — never commit credentials. Patterns are relative to the .gitignore's directory; ! re-includes.

languages.bash:

*.egg-info/
.pytest_cache/
.ruff_cache/

# Virtual environments
venv/
.venv/
env/

# Build artifacts

# IDE / editor

.idea/
*.swp
.DS_Store

# Logs / runtime
data/cache/
*.log
.env
*.pid

# Keep the .env.example template if you commit one:
!.env.example

intro: Here's a setup.py for a Python package.
notes: Modern projects prefer pyproject.toml (PEP 621) — setup.py still works but is legacy. For a simple package, setuptools with find_packages() is the standard layout.

languages.bash:
from setuptools import setup, find_packages

setup(
    name='my-package',
    version='0.1.0',
    description='A short description',
    packages=find_packages(exclude=['tests*']),
    python_requires='>=3.10',
    install_requires=[
        'requests>=2.31',
    ],
    extras_require={
        'dev': ['pytest', 'ruff'],
    },
    entry_points={
        'console_scripts': [
            'mycli=my_package.cli:main',
        ],
    },
)

# Modern equivalent: pyproject.toml
# [build-system]
# requires = ['setuptools>=61']
# build-backend = 'setuptools.build_meta'
#
# [project]
# name = 'my-package'
# version = '0.1.0'
# requires-python = '>=3.10'
# dependencies = ['requests>=2.31']

intro: Here's how to schedule a cron job that runs a script daily.
notes: crontab -e edits your user's schedule. The five fields are minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. Redirect output (>> log 2>&1) so cron errors are visible, and use absolute paths.

languages.bash:
# Edit your crontab:
#   crontab -e

# Run every day at 2:30am:
30 2 * * * /usr/bin/python3 /home/me/scripts/backup.py >> /home/me/backup.log 2>&1

# Every hour:
0 * * * * /home/me/scripts/hourly.sh

# Every Monday at 9am:
0 9 * * 1 /home/me/scripts/weekly_report.sh

# Every 15 minutes:
*/15 * * * * /home/me/scripts/ping.sh

# Field order: minute(0-59) hour(0-23) dom(1-31) month(1-12) dow(0-7, 0/7=Sun)

# List your jobs:
#   crontab -l

# Remove all your jobs:
#   crontab -r

# Scripts should use absolute paths and set their own PATH:
#!/bin/bash
cd /home/me && ./scripts/backup.py >> /home/me/backup.log 2>&1

intro: Here's a systemd service unit for a Python app.
notes: Units live in /etc/systemd/system/ (root) or ~/.config/systemd/user/. After writing one: systemctl daemon-reload, then enable --now. Restart=on-failure brings the app back automatically.

languages.bash:
# /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service
[Unit]
Description=My Python application
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=www-data
WorkingDirectory=/opt/myapp
EnvironmentFile=/etc/myapp.env
ExecStart=/opt/myapp/venv/bin/uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

# Hardening (optional but recommended):
NoNewPrivileges=true
PrivateTmp=true
ProtectSystem=full

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

# Commands:
#   sudo systemctl daemon-reload
#   sudo systemctl enable --now myapp
#   sudo systemctl status myapp
#   sudo journalctl -u myapp -f      # logs
#   sudo systemctl restart myapp

intro: Here's how to watch a file for changes in {lang}.
notes: inotifywait (inotify-tools) is the classic CLI watcher. For scripts, a polling loop with stat is portable; Python's watchdog library is the batteries-included option.

languages.bash:
# inotify-tools (apt install inotify-tools):
# Run a command every time a file in the directory changes:
inotifywait -m -r -e modify,create,delete /path/to/dir |
while read path event file; do
    echo "$event: $path$file"
    ./your-handler.sh "$path$file"
done

# Watch a single file:
inotifywait -m -e modify /var/log/app.log

# One-shot (exit after the first event):
inotifywait -e modify /var/log/app.log && echo changed

# Portable fallback: poll mtime every second
#!/bin/bash
LAST=$(stat -c %Y /path/to/file)
while true; do
    NOW=$(stat -c %Y /path/to/file)
    if [ "$NOW" != "$LAST" ]; then
        echo "file changed"
        LAST=$NOW
    fi
    sleep 1
done

intro: Here's how to compress a directory with tar in {lang}.
notes: tar -czf creates a gzipped archive; -xzf extracts. Always test with -tzf (list). Use -C to avoid storing absolute paths, and -z for gzip vs -j for bzip2.

languages.bash:
# Create a gzipped archive of a directory:
tar -czf myproject.tar.gz myproject/

# Extract it:
tar -xzf myproject.tar.gz

# List contents (verify before extracting):
tar -tzf myproject.tar.gz

# Compress from the parent dir so paths stay relative:
cd /home/me && tar -czf myproject.tar.gz myproject

# Exclude files:
tar -czf myproject.tar.gz --exclude='*.log' --exclude='node_modules' myproject

# bzip2 (smaller, slower):
tar -cjf myproject.tar.bz2 myproject

# Extract to a specific directory:
tar -xzf myproject.tar.gz -C /tmp

intro: Here's how to grep recursively for a pattern in {lang}.
notes: grep -r searches recursively; -n shows line numbers, -i ignores case, -l lists only filenames. Use rg (ripgrep) for speed — it respects .gitignore.

languages.bash:
# Recursive search in the current directory:
grep -rn "TODO" .

# Case-insensitive, with line numbers:
grep -rni "error" src/

# Only filenames containing the match:
grep -rl "FIXME" .

# Whole-word matches only:
grep -rnw "class" src/

# Extended regex (-E) or fixed strings (-F):
grep -rnE "error|fail" logs/
grep -rnF "literal.dots" .

# Exclude directories:
grep -rn "TODO" . --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.git

# Count matches per file:
grep -rc "error" logs/

# Ripgrep (faster, respects .gitignore):
rg -n "TODO" src/

intro: Here's how to show the last N lines of a log and follow new ones in {lang}.
notes: tail -n 50 shows the last 50 lines; tail -f (or -F — handles log rotation) follows new appends. Combine: tail -n 50 -f. head -n 50 shows the first lines.

languages.bash:
# Last 50 lines, then follow new output:
tail -n 50 -f app.log

# Just the last 50 lines (no follow):
tail -n 50 app.log

# Follow only (defaults to last 10 lines):
tail -f app.log

# Follow with retries — survives log rotation (-F):
tail -F app.log

# First 50 lines:
head -n 50 app.log

# Follow multiple files:
tail -f app.log web.log

# Filter what you follow:
tail -f app.log | grep --line-buffered ERROR

intro: Here's how to convert an MP4 to a GIF with ffmpeg in {lang}.
notes: GIFs are huge — keep the source short, scale it down, and drop the framerate. A palette-based conversion (two-pass) gives the best quality for the size.

languages.bash:
# Simple conversion:
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 output.gif

# Smaller, smoother (scale + framerate):
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -vf "fps=10,scale=480:-1:flags=lanczos" output.gif

# Best quality per byte (palette method):
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -vf "fps=10,scale=480:-1:flags=lanczos,palettegen" palette.png
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -i palette.png -lavfi "fps=10,scale=480:-1:flags=lanczos[x];[x][1:v]paletteuse" output.gif

# Loop only once (default is infinite):
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -loop 1 output.gif

# First 5 seconds only:
ffmpeg -ss 0 -t 5 -i input.mp4 output.gif

# Audio extraction:
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -q:a 0 -map a audio.mp3

intro: Here's how to find and delete files older than N days in {lang}.
notes: find -mtime +30 matches files modified more than 30 days ago. Test with -print first, then swap in -delete (or -exec rm {} +). -mtime counts 24h periods; -mmin works in minutes.

languages.bash:
# List files modified more than 30 days ago (dry run):
find /var/log -type f -mtime +30 -print

# Delete them:
find /var/log -type f -mtime +30 -delete

# Delete via exec (more portable, verbose):
find /var/log -type f -mtime +30 -exec rm {} \;

# Also remove now-empty directories:
find /var/log -type d -empty -delete

# Minutes instead of days:
find /tmp -type f -mmin +120 -delete

# Exclude a path:
find /var/log -type f -mtime +30 -not -path '*/important/*' -delete

# Combine with a file-size floor:
find . -type f -size +100M -mtime +30 -delete

intro: Here's how to sync a directory to a remote server with rsync in {lang}.
notes: rsync copies only changed files (delta transfer). Trailing slashes matter: src/ copies CONTENTS into dst; src copies the directory itself. -a preserves permissions and timestamps.

languages.bash:
# Push to a remote server:
rsync -avz ./project/ user@server:/srv/project/

# Pull from remote:
rsync -avz user@server:/srv/project/ ./project/

# -a archive (recursive + permissions), -v verbose, -z compress

# Dry run (see what WOULD transfer):
rsync -avzn ./project/ user@server:/srv/project/

# Delete files on the destination that no longer exist locally:
rsync -avz --delete ./project/ user@server:/srv/project/

# Exclude junk:
rsync -avz --exclude node_modules --exclude .git ./project/ user@server:/srv/project/

# Over SSH with a custom port:
rsync -avz -e 'ssh -p 2222' ./project/ user@server:/srv/project/

# Local mirror (e.g. backup to an external drive):
rsync -av --delete ~/Documents/ /mnt/backup/Documents/

intro: Here's how to loop over files in a directory in {lang}.
notes: The glob pattern approach handles spaces in filenames safely (quote "$f"). For recursive iteration use find ... | while read or ** globbing.

languages.bash:
#!/bin/bash
# Loop over every .txt file in the current directory:
for f in *.txt; do
    echo "processing $f"
    # wc -l "$f"   # quote "$f" — filenames may contain spaces!
done

# Loop over ALL files (not just a pattern):
for f in *; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue    # skip directories
    echo "$f"
done

# Recursive (find + while read):
find . -name '*.py' -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
    echo "$f"
done

# With a counter:
i=0
for f in *.log; do
    (( i++ ))
    echo "[$i] $f"
done

# Python version:
# import glob
# for path in glob.glob('*.txt'):
#     print(path)

intro: Here's how to extract text between quotes in {lang}.
notes: sed's capture group is the classic one-liner. grep -o prints only the matched part. In Python, a regex findall with a capture group returns just the quoted text.

languages.bash:
# Extract the FIRST quoted string (sed):
echo 'say "hello world" now' | sed -n 's/.*"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p'
# hello world

# Extract ALL quoted strings (grep -o):
echo 'a "one" b "two"' | grep -o '"[^"]*"'
# "one"
# "two"

# Single quotes:
echo "it's 'fine' really" | grep -o "'[^']*'"

# From a file:
grep -o '"[^"]*"' file.txt
languages.python:
import re

text = 'say "hello world" now and "bye"'

# All quoted strings (without the quotes):
print(re.findall(r'"([^"]*)"', text))
# ['hello world', 'bye']

# With the quotes:
print(re.findall(r'"[^"]*"', text))

# First match only:
m = re.search(r'"([^"]*)"', text)
print(m.group(1) if m else None)   # hello world

intro: Here's how to rename files (e.g. .txt → .md) in {lang}.
notes: The for-loop with parameter expansion ${f%.txt} strips the extension cleanly. Use rename(1) (the Perl tool) for complex renames, or mv for single files.

languages.bash:
# Rename all .txt files to .md (bash loop):
for f in *.txt; do
    mv -- "$f" "${f%.txt}.md"
done

# Dry run first (echo instead of mv):
for f in *.txt; do echo "$f -> ${f%.txt}.md"; done

# With the rename utility (Perl rename):
rename 's/\.txt$/.md/' *.txt

# Prefix every file:
for f in *.jpg; do mv -- "$f" "backup-$f"; done

# Recursive:
find . -name '*.txt' -exec bash -c 'mv "$1" "${1%.txt}.md"' _ {} \;
languages.python:
from pathlib import Path

# Rename every .txt file to .md in the current directory:
for path in Path('.').glob('*.txt'):
    path.rename(path.with_suffix('.md'))

# With a log:
for path in Path('.').glob('*.txt'):
    new = path.with_suffix('.md')
    print(f'{path} -> {new}')
    path.rename(new)

intro: Here's how to check pods with kubectl.
notes: kubectl get pods lists pods; add -n for a namespace, -o wide for node/IP, and -w to watch. Describe shows details and events; logs streams container output.

languages.bash:
# List pods in the default namespace:
kubectl get pods

# In a specific namespace:
kubectl get pods -n myapp

# All namespaces:
kubectl get pods -A

# More detail:
kubectl get pods -o wide

# Watch for changes:
kubectl get pods -w

# Describe one pod (events, status):
kubectl describe pod my-pod-abc123

# Logs:
kubectl logs my-pod-abc123
kubectl logs deployment/my-app -f    # follow

# Exec into a container:
kubectl exec -it my-pod-abc123 -- /bin/sh

intro: Here's a Kubernetes Deployment manifest.
notes: A Deployment manages replica Pods with rolling updates and self-healing. Apply with kubectl apply -f, scale with kubectl scale, and check rollout status with kubectl rollout status.

languages.bash:
# deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: myapp:1.0.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
          env:
            - name: APP_ENV
              value: production
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 512Mi
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8000

# Apply:  kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
# Scale:  kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5
# Status: kubectl rollout status deployment/web
# Update: kubectl set image deployment/web web=myapp:1.1.0
# Rollback: kubectl rollout undo deployment/web

intro: Here's an nginx config that serves a static site.
notes: The server block maps a domain to a root directory; try_files enables SPA-style clean URLs. Enable compression and cache headers for performance. Test with nginx -t before reloading.

intro: Here's a Docker multi-stage build.
notes: Multi-stage builds compile/build in one stage (with all the tooling) and copy only the artifacts into a slim final image — much smaller and safer. Each FROM starts a new stage; AS names it.

languages.bash:
# Dockerfile — Go example:
FROM golang:1.22 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app ./cmd/server

# Final stage: just the binary
FROM scratch
COPY --from=builder /app /app
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

# Python example:
# FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
#   ... pip install --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt
# FROM python:3.12-slim
# COPY --from=build /install /usr/local
#   ... copy app code, CMD ...

# Build: docker build -t myapp .
# Inspect stages: docker build --target builder -t myapp-builder .

intro: Here's how to extract a column from a file with awk.
notes: awk splits each line into fields: $1, $2, ... (FS default is whitespace). Set -F for a delimiter like a comma. Print with printf for aligned output.

languages.bash:
# Print the second column (whitespace-separated):
awk '{print $2}' data.txt

# CSV with -F:
awk -F, '{print $2}' data.csv

# Header + first two columns:
awk -F, 'NR==1 || NR>1 {print $1, $2}' data.csv

# Skip the header entirely:
awk -F, 'NR>1 {print $2}' data.csv

# Filter + column:
awk -F, '$3 > 100 {print $1}' data.csv

# Sum a column:
awk -F, '{sum += $2} END {print sum}' data.csv

# Formatted output:
awk '{printf "%-10s %5d\n", $1, $2}' data.txt

intro: Here's how to parse JSON in bash with jq.
notes: jq filters JSON: .field, .[index], .[] iterates, | pipes filters. Combine with curl for API output. Use -r for raw strings (no quotes).

languages.bash:
# Pretty-print:
cat data.json | jq .
curl -s https://api.example.com/data | jq .

# Extract a field:
echo '{"name": "alice", "age": 30}' | jq '.name'
# "alice"  (with -r: alice)

# Array element / iteration:
jq '.[0]' data.json        # first element
jq '.[].name' data.json    # name of each element

# Filtering:
jq '.[] | select(.age > 21)' data.json

# Transform:
jq '{users: [.[] | {n: .name, a: .age}]}' data.json

# Length / counts:
jq 'length' data.json

# Key lookup with default:
jq '.missing // "fallback"' data.json

intro: Here's how to run commands in parallel with xargs.
notes: xargs builds commands from stdin. -P sets parallelism, -n batches arguments, -0 handles newlines in filenames safely (pair with find -print0).

languages.bash:
# Run one command per line, 4 at a time:
cat urls.txt | xargs -P 4 -I {} curl -s {} -o /dev/null

# Process files, 4 in parallel:
find . -name '*.jpg' -print0 | xargs -0 -P 4 -n 1 sh -c 'convert "$0" "${0%.jpg}.png"'

# Batch arguments (-n 10 = 10 args per command):
ls *.txt | xargs -n 10 wc -l

# Replace token with -I:
seq 1 10 | xargs -P 5 -I {} echo 'job {}'

# Dry run (echo the commands):
seq 1 3 | xargs -I {} echo curl -s https://api.example.com/{}

intro: Here's how to replace text in a file with sed.
notes: sed 's/old/new/' replaces the first match per line; add g for all, i for case-insensitive, and -i to edit in place (use -i.bak to keep a backup).

languages.bash:
# Replace first occurrence per line (print to stdout):
sed 's/foo/bar/' file.txt

# Replace ALL occurrences:
sed 's/foo/bar/g' file.txt

# In place, with a backup:
sed -i.bak 's/foo/bar/g' file.txt

# In place, no backup (GNU sed):
sed -i 's/foo/bar/g' file.txt

# Case-insensitive:
sed -i 's/foo/bar/gi' file.txt

# Line-anchored:
sed -i '/^#/d' file.txt            # delete comment lines
sed -i '10,20s/foo/bar/g' file.txt # lines 10-20 only

# Escaping special chars:
sed -i 's|https://old|https://new|' file.txt   # | as delimiter

# macOS: sed -i '' 's/foo/bar/g' file.txt

intro: Here's how to sort a file by a column with sort.
notes: sort -k N sorts by the Nth field. Add -n for numeric, -r for reverse, -t to set the delimiter, and -u to dedupe. -h understands human sizes (1K, 2M).

languages.bash:
# Sort by the 2nd column (whitespace):
sort -k2 data.txt

# Numeric, descending:
sort -k2 -n -r data.txt

# CSV with a custom delimiter:
sort -t, -k2 -n data.csv

# Multiple keys (column 1, then 2):
sort -k1,1 -k2,2n data.txt

# Human-readable sizes (1K, 2M):
du -sh * | sort -k1 -h -r

# Deduplicate adjacent identical lines:
sort -u data.txt

# Sort with case-insensitive and unique:
sort -f -u data.txt

intro: Here's how to find duplicate lines in a file.
notes: sort + uniq -d shows lines that repeat; uniq -c counts occurrences. awk keeps the first-seen order without sorting.

languages.bash:
# Duplicate lines (requires sorted input):
sort file.txt | uniq -d

# Count occurrences:
sort file.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn

# Unique lines only:
sort file.txt | uniq

# Preserve first-seen order (awk):
awk 'seen[$0]++ {print}' file.txt          # dupes in order
awk '!seen[$0]++' file.txt                 # uniques in order

# Case-insensitive duplicates:
sort -f file.txt | uniq -di

intro: Here's a Terraform config that provisions an AWS EC2 instance.
notes: terraform init downloads providers; terraform plan previews changes; terraform apply creates resources. The ~/.aws/credentials file or AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY env vars supply credentials.

intro: Here's how to create and extract tar archives.
notes: tar -czf creates (c) a gzip (z) archive to a file (f); tar -xzf extracts it. Use tar -tf to list contents before extracting. Add v for verbose output.

languages.bash:
# Extract a tar.gz file:
tar -xzf archive.tar.gz

# List contents without extracting:
tar -tf archive.tar.gz

# Create a gzipped archive of a directory:
tar -czf archive.tar.gz my_folder/

# Plain .tar (no gzip): use -xf / -cf
tar -xf archive.tar

intro: Here's how to create a symbolic link in Linux.
notes: ln -s TARGET LINK makes LINK point at TARGET — order matters, target first. Use absolute paths to keep the link valid from other directories. rm LINK removes the link, never the target.

languages.bash:
# Create a symlink:  ln -s TARGET LINK
ln -s /data/shared /home/alice/shared

# Verify:
ls -l /home/alice/shared   # shows shared -> /data/shared

# Remove a symlink (the link, not the target):
rm /home/alice/shared

# Overwrite an existing link:
ln -sfn /data/new /home/alice/shared

intro: Here's how to loop over lines in a file in bash.
notes: while IFS= read -r line handles any line (spaces, backslashes) and is the recommended form; a for loop over $(cat file) breaks on spaces. The -r flag keeps backslashes literal.

languages.bash:
# Read a file line by line (safe with spaces/backslashes):
while IFS= read -r line; do
    echo "line: $line"
done < input.txt

# From a command's output:
find . -name '*.py' | while read -r f; do
    echo "processing $f"
done

intro: Here's how to use arrays in bash.
notes: arr=(a b c) creates an array; ${arr[0]} indexes, ${arr[@]} expands all elements, ${#arr[@]} is the length. Quote "${arr[@]}" to keep elements with spaces intact.

languages.bash:
# Create and use an array:
files=(a.txt "b c.txt" d.log)

echo "${files[0]}"        # a.txt
echo "${files[1]}"        # b c.txt
echo "${#files[@]}"       # 3 (length)
echo "${files[@]}"        # all elements

# Loop over elements (quotes preserve spaces):
for f in "${files[@]}"; do
    echo "-- $f"
done

intro: Here's how to use a here document in bash.
notes: cat <<EOF ... EOF feeds literal text to a command's stdin. Quote the marker (<<'EOF') to prevent variable/command expansion. Use <<- to allow indented markers with tabs.

languages.bash:
# Feed multi-line input to a command:
cat <<EOF
Hello, this is a here document.
Variables expand: $HOME
EOF

# Quoted marker = no expansion:
cat <<'EOF'
Literal text: $HOME stays as-is
EOF

# Write a file with heredoc:
cat > config.txt <<EOF
server = localhost
port = 8080
EOF

intro: Here's how to split a string in bash.
notes: IFS + read -ra splits into an array: IFS=',' read -ra parts <<< "$str". Bash 4+ has readarray -t lines < file for splitting by newlines. cut and awk handle simple field splitting.

languages.bash:
# Split on a delimiter into an array:
str="alice,bob,carol"
IFS=',' read -ra names <<< "$str"
echo "${names[0]}"    # alice
echo "${names[2]}"    # carol

# Split a file into lines (bash 4+):
readarray -t lines < input.txt

# Field split with cut (no array):
echo "a:b:c" | cut -d: -f2    # b

intro: Here's how to find files containing text with grep.
notes: grep -r searches recursively; -l lists filenames only; -n shows line numbers. grep -i ignores case, -E enables extended regex. ripgrep (rg) is faster and respects .gitignore.

languages.bash:
# Find files containing text, recursively:
grep -rl 'TODO' .                    # filenames only
grep -rn 'FIXME' src/                # with line numbers
grep -ri 'error' --include='*.py' .  # case-insensitive, only .py

# Invert match:
grep -L 'copyright' *.py             # files WITHOUT the text

# Modern alternative: rg (ripgrep)
rg -l 'TODO' .

intro: Here's how to view Docker container logs.
notes: docker logs <container> prints stdout/stderr; -f follows live, --tail N shows the last N lines. Use the container name or ID; docker ps lists them.

languages.bash:
# List containers:
docker ps

# View logs:
docker logs my-app
docker logs -f my-app          # follow live
docker logs --tail 100 my-app  # last 100 lines
docker logs --since 10m my-app # last 10 minutes

intro: Here's how to exec into a running Docker container.
notes: docker exec -it <container> <cmd> runs a command inside a running container; bash/sh gives you a shell. Add -u root for root, and -w to set the working directory. If the container has no bash, use sh.

languages.bash:
# Open a shell in a running container:
docker exec -it my-app bash
docker exec -it my-app sh     # if bash isn't installed

# Run a single command:
docker exec my-app ls /app

# As root, in a specific directory:
docker exec -it -u root -w /app my-app bash

intro: Here's how to pin dependencies in requirements.txt.
notes: pip freeze lists installed versions; redirect to a file to lock them. Use == for exact pins, >= for minimums with compatible-release (~=) when you want updates. For applications, pin exactly; for libraries, allow ranges.

languages.bash:
# Lock every installed package to its exact version:
pip freeze > requirements.txt

# requirements.txt uses == for exact pins:
#   flask==3.0.3
#   requests==2.32.3
#   sqlalchemy>=2.0,<2.1
#   black~=24.4.0        # >=24.4.0, <25.0.0

# Install from the lockfile:
pip install -r requirements.txt
